title: Reflections on AI Going Into This School Year
author: The Broken Copier
summary: A teacher at The Broken Copier processes a month of AI-in-education conversations, anchored by the Humans First: Adolescent Education in the Age of AI conference in Atlanta, into four takeaways for the coming school year. The opening keynote on Critical AI Literacy by Katie Conrad and Sean Kamperman convinced the author that AI literacy must treat AI as "a text to be understood," with sustained ethical scrutiny, rather than passively accepted as inevitable and merely taught as a tool -- a distinction he contrasts with the shallow "checklist disclosure" common at AI conferences. A second keynote by frequently-cited AI-in-writing researcher Marc Watkins reinforced a stance of humility about AI's unpredictable trajectory over the next three to five years, even as Watkins himself continues to build AI fluency and explore its instructional uses. The piece's most affecting moment comes from a student panel, where one student explained abandoning AI in their own learning entirely after concluding, "I lost my confidence in my own writing," having felt pressured toward AI use and toward prioritizing grades over actual learning -- evidence, the author argues, that students are already registering the costs adults are still debating in the abstract. He closes with his own decision to keep AI out of his classroom for now, and a broader appeal that education's problems, AI-related or not, are best faced through more conversation with colleagues rather than in isolation.
points: Drawing on keynote speakers Katie Conrad and Sean Kamperman, the author distinguishes an AI Literacy that passively accepts AI's trajectory as inevitable from a Critical AI Literacy that treats AI as "a text to be understood" through a sustained systems and ethics lens -- and commits to building the latter into his own classroom.

A student panelist's admission that they abandoned AI in their own learning because "I lost my confidence in my own writing," having felt pressured toward AI use and toward prioritizing grades over learning, becomes the piece's central evidence that AI's classroom costs are not hypothetical.

Citing AI researcher Marc Watkins's own presentation on AI's unpredictable development curve, the author argues humility about AI's next three-to-five years should run alongside continued engagement, not replace it.

The author's own concrete decision for the new school year is to continue keeping AI out of his own classroom as a learning tool, judging the costs described by his students not worth the trade-off for now.
quotes: There is a difference between a version of (1) an AI Literacy that implicitly suggests passive acceptance of the current trajectory and presumes inevitability of what AI's implementation will look like versus (2) a Critical AI Literacy that holds a system lens and ethics focus, treating AI like a text to be understood rather than just a tool to be learned.

It is powerful to avoid the "checklist disclosure" that too often shows up in AI presentations and conversations: a quick acknowledgment of critiques without spending any time actually sitting with and considering them.
We need to be humble about what we know about AI and its impact right now, yes, but even more so about what the next 3-5 years will look like - not to mention anything further down the road.
In explaining what led to this decision, this is what they said: "I lost my confidence in my own writing." You could immediately feel these words immediately sink into everyone listening.

That students are recognizing these AI tools are not good for their learning but still are choosing to use them should serve as a red alert about the signals we are sending within our classrooms and schools.

Our first survival instinct was with each other." Stepping into a new school year that inevitably will bring more challenges, around AI as well as myriad challenges beyond AI, I think it's fair to predict that the Sisyphean nature of education's problems outpacing its solutions will continue on, regardless of our context.
